title: Activity Selection Problem
description: Learn how **greedy scheduling** selects the maximum number of non-overlapping activities through **earliest-finish-time optimization**.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The **Activity Selection Problem** is one of the most well-known applications of Greedy Algorithms.[cite: 13]
*   You are given a set of activities, each with a **start time** and a **finish time**.[cite: 13]
*   Only one activity can be performed at a time, so you **cannot have overlapping activities**.[cite: 13]
*   The goal is to select the **maximum number of non-overlapping activities**.[cite: 13]

Imagine you are a conference organizer with one meeting room:[cite: 13]
1.  You receive multiple session requests, each with a start and end time.[cite: 13]
2.  You want to schedule **as many sessions as possible**.[cite: 13]
3.  Which sessions should you choose?[cite: 13] The greedy answer is to **always pick the session that ends earliest** because this leaves the most remaining time for other sessions.[cite: 13]

This problem demonstrates how local greedy decisions can produce **globally optimal scheduling solutions**.[cite: 13] It is a perfect example of when greedy works and why.[cite: 13]

The earliest-finish-first strategy is counterintuitive to some people who might think earliest start is better, but it is **provably optimal**.[cite: 13] This problem is a classic in computer science and appears in many real-world scheduling applications.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems involve scheduling limited resources.[cite: 13] Classrooms, airport runways, meeting rooms, CPU processors, and manufacturing systems **cannot handle multiple overlapping tasks simultaneously**.[cite: 13] Efficient scheduling improves productivity, resource usage, and execution efficiency.[cite: 13]

Examples of scheduling challenges:[cite: 13]
*   A university with one lecture hall needs to **schedule as many classes as possible** without overlap.[cite: 13]
*   An airport runway can only handle one plane at a time, so it needs to **maximize takeoff and landing slots**.[cite: 13]
*   A single-core processor receives jobs and must **maximize the number completed**.[cite: 13]

Poor scheduling leads to wasted resources like empty classrooms, idle runways, or unused CPU cycles.[cite: 13] Greedy scheduling maximizes utilization without complex computation.[cite: 13]

The Activity Selection Problem models this challenge computationally.[cite: 13] It provides an **optimal solution strategy** that is both fast and easy to implement.[cite: 13] Understanding this problem helps you solve many real-world scheduling challenges.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Let us define the problem formally:[cite: 13]
*   You are given a set of activities, each defined by a **start time and finish time**, where start time is less than finish time.[cite: 13]
*   The goal is to select a **maximum-size subset of activities** where no two activities overlap.[cite: 13]

**Two activities are compatible if they do not overlap.**[cite: 13] That means one finishes before or exactly when the other starts.[cite: 13] For example, activity A1 from 1 to 4 and activity A4 from 5 to 7 are compatible because 4 is less than or equal to 5.[cite: 13]

Consider these example activities:[cite: 13]
1.  **A1** is from 1 to 4.[cite: 13]
2.  **A2** is from 3 to 5.[cite: 13]
3.  **A3** is from 0 to 6.[cite: 13]
4.  **A4** is from 5 to 7.[cite: 13]
5.  **A5** is from 8 to 9.[cite: 13]

The objective is to select the **maximum number of compatible activities**.[cite: 13] Two activities are compatible if their time intervals do not overlap.[cite: 13] Understanding this compatibility condition is the foundation of the algorithm.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Understanding Overlapping Activities
sections.content:
To build intuition, let us examine how overlaps work and why careful selection matters.[cite: 13] Two intervals `[s1, f1]` and `[s2, f2]` overlap if they share any time in common.[cite: 13] For compatibility, we require that **one ends before or exactly when the other starts**.[cite: 13]

Using the previous example:
*   Suppose we first select **activity A1** from 1 to 4.[cite: 13]
*   **Activity A2** from 3 to 5 *cannot be selected* after A1 because A2 starts at 3 and A1 finishes at 4. Since 3 is less than 4, A2 begins before A1 finishes. This creates a scheduling conflict.[cite: 13]
*   **Activity A3** from 0 to 6 also overlaps with A1 because A3 starts before A1 and ends after A1 starts.[cite: 13]
*   **Activity A4** from 5 to 7 is *compatible* with A1 because 5 is greater than or equal to 4.[cite: 13]
*   **Activity A5** from 8 to 9 is *compatible* with A4 if A4 is selected because 8 is greater than or equal to 7.[cite: 13]

If you choose a long activity early, you **block many others**.[cite: 13] If you choose a short, early-finishing activity, you **preserve flexibility**.[cite: 13] This is the core intuition behind earliest-finish-first greedy.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Core Greedy Idea
sections.content:
The greedy strategy is simple. **Always select the activity that finishes earliest** among the remaining compatible activities.[cite: 13]

Follow these steps:[cite: 13]
1.  First, **sort all activities** by their finish time in ascending order.[cite: 13]
2.  **Select the first activity** in the sorted list, which is the one that finishes earliest.[cite: 13]
3.  For each subsequent activity in sorted order, if its start time is **greater than or equal to** the last selected activity's finish time, select it.[cite: 13]
4.  Otherwise, **skip it** because it overlaps.[cite: 13]

At first, this may seem unusual. Why not select the earliest starting activity?[cite: 13]
*   Consider Activity X from 1 to 100: It starts early but runs very long.[cite: 13]
*   Consider Activity Y from 2 to 3: It starts slightly later but finishes very quickly.[cite: 13]
*   If you pick X, you **block everything else**.[cite: 13] If you pick Y, you finish at time 3 and can **still schedule many more activities**.[cite: 13]

Choosing the earliest finishing activity **maximizes the remaining time available** for future activities.[cite: 13] This increases the chance of selecting additional compatible activities later.[cite: 13] Early finishing preserves scheduling flexibility.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Why Earliest Finishing Works
sections.content:
The greedy strategy works for activity selection because it satisfies the **Greedy Choice Property**.[cite: 13]

*   Suppose we select an activity that finishes very late, such as from 1 to 10. This **blocks many future activities**.[cite: 13] The schedule would have one long activity and then nothing else.[cite: 13]
*   However, if we instead choose an activity that finishes early, such as from 1 to 3, **more scheduling space remains afterward**.[cite: 13] You can then fit additional activities in the remaining time from 3 to infinity.[cite: 13]

There exists an optimal solution that includes the activity with the earliest finish time.[cite: 13]
*   Consider any optimal solution.[cite: 13]
*   If it already contains the earliest finishing activity, done.[cite: 13]
*   If it contains some other activity `k` as its first activity, since the earliest finishing activity finishes earlier or at the same time, we can **replace activity k with the earliest finishing activity**.[cite: 13]
*   This replacement does not cause any conflicts and the number of activities remains the same.[cite: 13]

Once we select the earliest finishing activity, we remove all activities that overlap with it.[cite: 13] The remaining problem is the same type, so the greedy choice can be applied again.[cite: 13] This is why the greedy strategy works correctly for this problem.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Example
sections.content:
Let us walk through the complete algorithm with detailed tracing.[cite: 13]
The unsorted activities are `A1 (1,4)`, `A2 (3,5)`, `A3 (0,6)`, `A4 (5,7)`, and `A5 (8,9)`.[cite: 13]

**Step 1: Sort by finish time**[cite: 13]
*   The sorted order becomes `A1(1,4)`, `A2(3,5)`, `A3(0,6)`, `A4(5,7)`, `A5(8,9)`.[cite: 13]

**Step 2: Initialize variables**[cite: 13]
*   Set `last_finish` to -1 and `selected` to an empty list.[cite: 13]

**Step 3: Iterate through activities**[cite: 13]
*   **Check A1 (1,4):** Is 1 greater than or equal to -1? Yes. **Select A1.** Update `last_finish` to 4.[cite: 13]
*   **Check A2 (3,5):** Is 3 greater than or equal to 4? No. A2 overlaps, so **skip it**.[cite: 13]
*   **Check A3 (0,6):** Is 0 greater than or equal to 4? No. A3 overlaps, so **skip it**.[cite: 13]
*   **Check A4 (5,7):** Is 5 greater than or equal to 4? Yes. **Select A4.** Update `last_finish` to 7.[cite: 13]
*   **Check A5 (8,9):** Is 8 greater than or equal to 7? Yes. **Select A5.** Update `last_finish` to 9.[cite: 13]

**Final Result:**[cite: 13]
*   The final selected activities are A1 from 1 to 4, A4 from 5 to 7, and A5 from 8 to 9.[cite: 13]
*   **Total activities selected is 3**.[cite: 13]
*   If we had chosen earliest start time, we would pick A3 first and get only 1 activity.[cite: 13] Earliest finish works because it leaves the maximum remaining time.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Timeline Visualization
sections.content:
Visualizing activity intervals helps explain overlap detection and scheduling compatibility.[cite: 13]
Let us represent the activities graphically:[cite: 13]
*   A1 runs from 1 to 4.[cite: 13]
*   A2 runs from 3 to 5.[cite: 13]
*   A3 runs from 0 to 6.[cite: 13]
*   A4 runs from 5 to 7.[cite: 13]
*   A5 runs from 8 to 9.[cite: 13]

After sorting by finish time, the order is **A1, A2, A3, A4, A5**.[cite: 13]
The greedy selection process flows as follows:[cite: 13]
1.  First selects **A1**.[cite: 13]
2.  Then **A2 overlaps** with A1 because it starts at 3 which is before A1 finishes at 4, so skip.[cite: 13]
3.  **A3 also overlaps**, so skip.[cite: 13]
4.  **A4 is compatible** because it starts at 5 which is after A1 finishes at 4, so select A4.[cite: 13]
5.  **A5 is compatible** because it starts at 8 which is after A4 finishes at 7, so select A5.[cite: 13]

The final selected schedule is A1 from 1 to 4, then A4 from 5 to 7, then A5 from 8 to 9.[cite: 13]
The visualization shows how compatible activities avoid overlap.[cite: 13] The gaps between activities represent idle time that is necessary because no activities fit in those gaps.[cite: 13] The algorithm **maximizes count, not utilization**.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
Activity Selection implementations usually **sort activities by finish time** before greedily selecting compatible intervals.[cite: 13] The basic version returns the list of selected activities.[cite: 13]

1.  First, sort activities by finish time in ascending order using the `key` parameter with a lambda function that returns the finish time.[cite: 13]
2.  Then initialize `selected` as an empty list and `last_finish` to negative infinity (or -1 if times are non-negative).[cite: 13]
3.  For each activity in sorted order, check if the start time is greater than or equal to `last_finish`.[cite: 13]
4.  If yes, the activity is compatible. Append it to `selected` and update `last_finish` to its finish time.[cite: 13]
5.  If no, skip the activity because it overlaps.[cite: 13]

The **count only version** returns the number of activities selected instead of the list, which is more memory efficient.[cite: 13]
The compatibility checking function demonstrates how to test if two activities overlap.[cite: 13] Two activities are compatible if one finishes before or exactly when the other starts.[cite: 13]

The examples below show these different implementations.[cite: 13]

codeSnippets.title: Activity Selection implementation
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [
    (1, 4),
    (3, 5),
    (0, 6),
    (5, 7),
    (8, 9)
]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

selected = []
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        selected.append((start, finish))
        last_finish = finish

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Count compatible activities
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (4, 6), (6, 8)]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

count = 0
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        count += 1
        last_finish = finish

print(count)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Analyzing the time and space complexity reveals why the greedy approach is optimal:[cite: 13]

*   **Sorting Step:** Sorting activities by finish time requires **O(n log n)** time.[cite: 13] This dominates the runtime for large n. Python's Timsort is efficient with O(n log n) worst case.[cite: 13]
*   **Selection Step:** After sorting, the algorithm performs only one linear traversal to select compatible activities. This is **O(n)** time.[cite: 13] Each activity is examined exactly once.[cite: 13]
*   **Total Time Complexity:** The total time complexity is **O(n log n)**.[cite: 13]

*   **Space Complexity:** Space complexity is **O(1)** for the count only version because only a few tracking variables are required.[cite: 13] The version storing selected activities uses **O(k)** space where `k` is the number of selected activities, which is at most n.[cite: 13]

A brute-force solution would try all `2^n` subsets and check each for conflicts, taking **O(2^n) time**, which is impossible for large n.[cite: 13] The greedy algorithm is exponentially faster.[cite: 13]

The chart below compares O(n), O(n log n), and O(n squared).[cite: 13] Sorting dominates, but O(n log n) is very efficient and scales well even for millions of activities.[cite: 13]

chart.title: Activity Selection complexity
chart.description: Sorting dominates the runtime of Activity Selection, while compatibility checking only requires linear traversal afterward.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Why This Problem Is Greedy
sections.content:
The Activity Selection Problem satisfies both properties needed for a greedy algorithm to be optimal.[cite: 13] These are the **Greedy Choice Property** and **Optimal Substructure**.[cite: 13]

**Greedy Choice Property:**[cite: 13]
*   There exists an optimal solution that includes the activity with the earliest finish time.[cite: 13]
*   If an optimal solution does not include the earliest finishing activity, replace its first activity with the earliest finishing one.[cite: 13]
*   This does not cause conflicts and gives the same number of activities.[cite: 13]

**Optimal Substructure:**[cite: 13]
*   After choosing the earliest finishing activity, the remaining problem, which consists of activities that start after it finishes, is a **smaller instance of the same problem**.[cite: 13]
*   The optimal solution for the whole problem contains optimal solutions for these subproblems.[cite: 13]

Choosing the earliest finishing activity **never reduces future scheduling opportunities**.[cite: 13] Early finishing preserves the maximum remaining time for additional compatible activities.[cite: 13] Any other choice would finish later, leaving less or equal time for subsequent activities.[cite: 13]

This is why the greedy strategy works correctly for this problem.[cite: 13] The problem structure ensures that **local optimality (earliest finish)** leads to **global optimality (maximum count)**.[cite: 13] Not all scheduling problems have this property, but activity selection does.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The Activity Selection Problem appears in CPU scheduling, classroom scheduling, airline runway allocation, manufacturing systems, operating systems, conference management, and cloud infrastructure scheduling.[cite: 13]

*   **CPU scheduling:** Shortest Job First and Earliest Deadline First use similar greedy principles.[cite: 13]
*   **Classroom scheduling:** A university with one lecture hall can schedule the maximum number of classes using this algorithm.[cite: 13]
*   **Airport allocation:** An airport with one runway can maximize takeoff and landing slots.[cite: 13]
*   **Booking systems:** A conference room booking system can maximize the number of meetings scheduled per day.[cite: 13]
*   **Manufacturing:** A manufacturing system with a single machine can maximize the number of jobs completed.[cite: 13]
*   **Media recording:** A television show recorder can record as many shows as possible on one channel.[cite: 13]

Many modern scheduling systems rely heavily on greedy optimization strategies.[cite: 13] The basic activity selection can be extended to **weighted activity selection** where each activity has a weight and you maximize total weight, but that requires dynamic programming.[cite: 13] Multiple resources like multiple rooms or processors require different algorithms.[cite: 13] However, the simple greedy algorithm for maximizing count is widely used because it is **fast, optimal, and easy to implement**.[cite: 13]

subsections.title: Mistake: Selecting earliest starting activities
subsections.content: Starting earlier **does not guarantee maximum scheduling flexibility**.[cite: 13] A long activity that starts early can block many subsequent activities.[cite: 13] The correct greedy choice is earliest finish time, not earliest start.[cite: 13]

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring sorting
subsections.content: The greedy strategy **depends on finish-time ordering**.[cite: 13] If activities are processed in arbitrary order, the algorithm may not find the optimal solution.[cite: 13] Always sort activities by finish time in ascending order as the first step.[cite: 13]

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect overlap checking
subsections.content: Activities are compatible if `current.start >= last_finish`.[cite: 13] Using greater than (`>`) without equal would reject activities that start exactly when the previous finishes, unnecessarily reducing the schedule.[cite: 13] **Use greater than or equal (`>=`)** to allow back-to-back scheduling.[cite: 13]

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The Activity Selection Problem **maximizes compatible activities**.[cite: 13]
The greedy strategy selects the **earliest finishing activity first**.[cite: 13]
The algorithm achieves **O(n log n)** complexity.[cite: 13]

references.title: Kleinberg, J., & Tardos, E. (2005). Algorithm Design. Pearson Education.
